title: One Magpie
subtitle: British folk superstition
summary: In British folk tradition, seeing a single magpie is associated with sorrow or bad luck. Entire rituals developed around politely greeting the bird, as if fate might be negotiated with good manners.

title: Two Magpies
subtitle: British folk superstition
summary: Where one magpie brings sorrow, two are traditionally said to bring joy. The rhyme turns birdwatching into a small act of divination, which is exactly the sort of behaviour humans would invent around a very smug corvid.

title: Ravens at the House
subtitle: British and European folk omen
summary: Ravens gathering near a house have often been read as a warning of death or misfortune. This is possibly unfair to ravens, who may simply enjoy rooftops and dramatic timing.

title: The Owl's Call
subtitle: Nocturnal folk omen
summary: An owl calling at night has long been treated as an uneasy sound in folklore. Depending on the place and teller, it might warn of death, spirits, illness, or merely that an owl is being extremely on brand.

title: Bird at the Window
subtitle: Household omen
summary: A bird striking or tapping at a window has often been interpreted as a message from beyond, or as a warning that death is near. It is one of those beliefs that turns ordinary glass into a very tense communication device.

title: Black Cat Crossing
subtitle: Animal luck omen
summary: The black cat is a folkloric overachiever: lucky in some British traditions, unlucky in others, and suspiciously elegant in all of them. A cat crossing your path may therefore be either a blessing or a tiny velvet audit.

title: Black Cat Entering the House
subtitle: Household luck superstition
summary: In parts of Britain, a black cat entering the home was considered a sign of good fortune. The cat, naturally, would not explain whether it had brought luck or merely noticed an available chair.

title: The Hare Crossing Your Path
subtitle: British witchcraft omen
summary: Hares occupy a strange place in British folklore, often linked with witches, shape-shifting, and uncanny night activity. A hare crossing your path was not always treated as innocent countryside business.

title: The White Hare
subtitle: Spirit animal folklore
summary: A white hare is sometimes treated in folklore as an otherworldly creature, spirit, or transformed witch. This is quite a lot of responsibility for a rabbit-shaped animal trying to cross a field.

title: Fox Crossing the Road
subtitle: Animal warning omen
summary: A fox crossing your path may be read as a warning, a trickster sign, or a prompt to pay attention. Foxes are already excellent at looking like they know something you do not.

title: Crows Gathering
subtitle: Corvid omen
summary: A gathering of crows has often made people nervous, especially when they appear suddenly or noisily. The birds may be discussing food, territory, or your general vibe.

title: Robin in the House
subtitle: Spirit visitation omen
summary: A robin entering the house has sometimes been interpreted as a sign of death or a visit from the spirit world. The robin, being small and red-breasted, manages to be both adorable and narratively alarming.

title: Moth in the House
subtitle: Soul visitor folklore
summary: Moths appearing indoors have often been linked with souls, visitors, or messages from the dead. They also have a talent for arriving at lamps like tiny haunted scraps of velvet.

title: Butterfly Indoors
subtitle: Visitor omen
summary: A butterfly entering the home may be read as a sign of a visitor, change, or a passing soul. Unlike many omens, this one arrives dressed beautifully and causes only mild confusion near the curtains.

title: Telling the Bees
subtitle: British death custom
summary: In parts of Britain, bees were formally told when a member of the household died. If neglected, the bees might leave, stop producing honey, or otherwise express their disappointment in the family administration.

title: Dogs Howling at Night
subtitle: Death omen
summary: Dogs howling at night have often been treated as warnings of death, illness, or restless spirits. Humans have always been deeply suspicious when animals notice things first.

title: Horses Sensing Spirits
subtitle: Animal sensitivity folklore
summary: Horses were often believed to sense ghosts, fairies, or danger before humans could. This is plausible enough in folklore terms: horses are large, emotional, and constantly one suspicious leaf away from prophecy.

title: Toads and Witches
subtitle: Witchcraft familiar folklore
summary: Toads were often associated with witches, poisons, and familiars in European folklore. This is extremely rude to toads, who mostly seem interested in dampness and being left alone.

title: Frogs Bringing Rain
subtitle: Weather superstition
summary: Frogs have often been linked to rain, damp weather, and seasonal change. If frogs are noisy, active, or suddenly abundant, folk wisdom may decide the sky is about to get involved.

title: Spider Luck
subtitle: Household creature superstition
summary: Spiders in the house are sometimes treated as lucky, especially if left unharmed. This may be folklore's way of encouraging people not to evict tiny unpaid pest-control staff.

title: Broken Mirror
subtitle: Household bad luck superstition
summary: Breaking a mirror is said to bring seven years of bad luck. The belief likely draws on the idea that mirrors reflect more than appearances, which is exactly the sort of thing mirrors would do if given the chance.

title: Umbrella Indoors
subtitle: Household bad luck superstition
summary: Opening an umbrella indoors is widely considered unlucky. It is also impractical, faintly aggressive, and probably a good way to offend both furniture and fate.

title: Spilled Salt
subtitle: Household bad luck superstition
summary: Spilling salt has long been considered unlucky, partly because salt was once valuable and partly because humans enjoy assigning cosmic meaning to table accidents. The traditional countermeasure is to toss some over the left shoulder.

title: Salt Over the Left Shoulder
subtitle: Protective household charm
summary: Throwing spilled salt over the left shoulder is meant to ward off bad luck or blind the devil lurking there. It is a tidy example of folk magic disguised as seasoning management.

title: Shoes on the Table
subtitle: Household death omen
summary: Putting shoes on a table is often treated as bad luck, and in some traditions as an omen of death. It is also, separately, an offence against hygiene and common sense.

title: New Shoes on a Table
subtitle: Particularly cursed domestic etiquette
summary: New shoes placed on a table are sometimes considered especially unlucky. The belief is often linked with death customs, though it may also reflect a deep ancestral certainty that tables are not for footwear.

title: Sweeping Over Feet
subtitle: Marriage superstition
summary: Sweeping a broom over someone's feet is said to prevent them from marrying, at least in some domestic folklore. This gives ordinary floor cleaning a surprising amount of romantic authority.

title: Crossed Knives
subtitle: Quarrel omen
summary: Crossed knives on a table are traditionally said to invite arguments or conflict. Cutlery, it turns out, should not be arranged like tiny declarations of war.

title: Candle Going Out
subtitle: Spirit presence omen
summary: A candle going out unexpectedly has often been taken as a sign of spirits, death, or unseen presence. This is atmospheric, inconvenient, and exactly why candles should not be trusted with narrative timing.

title: Clock Stopping at Death
subtitle: Death household custom
summary: Stopping clocks after a death was a known mourning custom, and a clock stopping by itself could be read as an omen. Few household objects are as dramatic as a timepiece deciding the story is over.

title: Covering Mirrors After Death
subtitle: Mourning custom
summary: Mirrors were often covered after a death to prevent spirits from being trapped, to mark mourning, or to keep the household spiritually tidy. It is a beautifully eerie example of grief reorganising the furniture.

title: The Empty Rocking Chair
subtitle: Ghostly household sign
summary: An empty rocking chair moving by itself is a classic ghostly image, treated in folklore as a sign of unseen presence. It is also proof that furniture should not be allowed to move independently after dusk.

title: Post-Mortem Portraits
subtitle: Mourning-adjacent custom
summary: Victorian post-mortem photography was not simply superstition, but it belongs near the same candlelit shelf. Families used photographs to preserve memory, producing images that now feel both tender and deeply uncanny.

title: Rowan Wood
subtitle: Protective tree charm
summary: Rowan trees have long been associated with protection against witches, evil, and misfortune. A sprig of rowan near a door or stable was folk security software, but prettier.

title: Iron Above the Door
subtitle: Protection against fairies and witches
summary: Iron was widely believed to repel fairies, witches, and harmful forces. Placing iron near thresholds turned ordinary doorways into tiny defensive borders against the unseen.

title: Horseshoe Over the Door
subtitle: Household luck charm
summary: A horseshoe over the door is one of the best-known protective charms. Hung upright, it may hold luck like a cup; hung downward, it may pour luck over the household, which is generous but logistically debated.

title: Garlic Against Evil
subtitle: Protective plant charm
summary: Garlic has long been used in European folk belief as protection against evil, illness, and inconvenient supernatural visitors. Its strongest documented power may be making a room smell aggressively defended.

title: Bells Against Spirits
subtitle: Sound-based protection
summary: Bells have often been rung to drive away spirits, evil, storms, or general bad influence. Folk belief apparently decided that unseen forces dislike being loudly informed they are unwelcome.

title: Clothes Inside Out
subtitle: Fairy confusion charm
summary: Turning clothes inside out was sometimes used to break fairy enchantment, avoid being led astray, or confuse supernatural mischief. It is a pleasingly low-budget defence against the otherworld.

title: Hag Stones
subtitle: Protective stone charm
summary: A hag stone is a naturally holed stone, often kept as protection against witches, nightmares, or ill luck. Looking through the hole was sometimes said to reveal hidden things, because apparently even rocks can become surveillance equipment.

title: Witch Marks
subtitle: Protective building marks
summary: Protective marks carved into buildings were meant to guard against witches, spirits, or bad fortune entering the home. They are tiny architectural spells, hidden in beams, thresholds, and old walls.

title: Red Thread
subtitle: Protective thread charm
summary: Red thread or cord has been used in many folk traditions as protection against harm, envy, or bad luck. It is small, portable, and satisfyingly dramatic for something that can fit in a pocket.

title: Coins in Shoes
subtitle: Luck charm
summary: Coins placed in shoes are associated with luck, prosperity, and safe passage in various folk customs. This is either magical thinking or the earliest known loyalty points scheme for feet.

title: The Scottish Play
subtitle: Theatre superstition
summary: Saying the name of Macbeth inside a theatre is famously considered unlucky, so performers often call it 'the Scottish Play' instead. Theatre people may reject many things, but not a good operational superstition.

title: Corpse Roads
subtitle: Funeral path folklore
summary: Corpse roads were routes used to carry the dead to burial, and folklore often treated them as spiritually charged paths. A landscape becomes much more dramatic once even the roads have a memory of the dead.

title: Midnight Churchyard Divination
subtitle: Spooky folk practice
summary: Churchyards at midnight appear frequently in divination and ghost folklore, especially for glimpsing future lovers or future deaths. This is a terrible time and place to conduct personal admin, which is probably why folklore liked it.

title: Mirror at Midnight
subtitle: Divination superstition
summary: Looking into a mirror at midnight appears in several traditions of divination and ghostly summoning. The basic premise is that mirrors become more opinionated after dark.

title: Black Dog Sightings
subtitle: British spectral animal lore
summary: Ghostly black dogs haunt British folklore, often appearing on roads, moors, churchyards, or lonely paths. They may be guardians, omens, or very large reasons to go home immediately.

title: The Fetch
subtitle: Double-sighting omen
summary: A fetch is a supernatural double of a living person, often seen as an omen of illness or death. Folklore has a real talent for making even seeing yourself feel like bad customer service from reality.

title: Deathwatch Beetle
subtitle: Insect death omen
summary: The tapping sound of the deathwatch beetle was once heard as an omen of death, especially in quiet old houses. The beetle was probably just looking for a mate, but folklore had already written the gothic version.
